extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students learning the logic of induction and experimental method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and procedures for judging when observed regularities constitute empirical laws, how to detect causal connections rather than chance coincidences, and how to eliminate chance by experimental design and averaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws are only true within observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can only be received as true within the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which they have been found true by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because empirical laws may depend on collocations of conditions that are not governed by any known law, they cannot safely be extended beyond the circumstances in which they have been observed. Example: the order of strata producing coal-beds on Earth cannot be assumed to hold on the moon or other planets because the necessary collocation of causes may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone proves only empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: No generalization rests on more than an empirical law when the only proof is the Method of Agreement, since that method cannot determine causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Agreement identifies the whole of the circumstances common to cases where a phenomenon occurs but cannot distinguish which of those uniformities are laws of causation versus derivative uniformities or collateral effects. Such results must be confirmed either by the Method of Difference or by deductive (a priori) explanation before being treated as causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs that a law of causation is derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of causation (even if ascertained) may be derivative rather than ultimate if there are indications of intermediate links or if the antecedent is extremely complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First sign: evidence of an intermediate phenomenon (x) between antecedent a and consequent b suggests a is a remote cause and the law a → b is resolvable into a → x and x → b (example: chemical combination producing water involves unseen corpuscular processes). Second sign: complex antecedents composed of multiple elements suggest the observed effect may be compound (composition of causes), as in meteorological sequences; such cases are likely resolvable into simpler laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of causes undermines simple agreement-based inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a phenomenon may have many possible causes, coincident antecedents found by agreement may be accidental; frequency of repetition reduces but does not eliminate this uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coincidence may recur often and yet be casual; recurrence alone does not prove a law. One must assess whether a coincidence occurs more often than chance would predict given the individual frequencies of the phenomena (see marginal-frequency calculation). Example anti-pattern: treating constant co-existence (e.g., fixed stars and all observed phenomena) as causal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate coincidences against expected frequency from marginals
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether a coincidence indicates a law, deduct from observed coincidence the amount expected from the absolute frequencies of each phenomenon occurring independently; any excess is evidence for connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute expected joint frequency from marginal frequencies (example: A in 1/2 of cases and B in 1/3 → expected A & B in 1/6). If observed co-occurrence exceeds this expectation, infer some causal connection; if it is less, infer repugnance or counteracting causes. Examples: rain and winds—compare co-occurrence rates adjusted for how often each wind blows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-proportion criterion for inferring connection
rubrics_metrics.description: If A occurs in a larger proportion of the cases where B is than of the cases where B is not (equivalently, B occurs more often where A is than where A is not), then there is a causal connection (empirically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparative-proportion test is symmetric and implies that, at some stage of analysis, common causes or causal relations should be discoverable. Until explained a priori, such a connection remains an empirical law. Use contingency comparison rather than raw counts to control for base rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes: isolate constant cause by many trials with mean
rubrics_metrics.description: When a constant cause A produces an effect that is habitually modified by many variable causes, preserve A in repeated trials and take the mean of results; the average approximates the effect due to A alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If repeated experiments (varying the incidental causes) oscillate around a stable mean which further trials do not materially change, that mean represents the constant cause's effect. This method is necessary when we cannot exclude all variable causes. Examples: averaging repeated experimental measurements; determining temperature trends amid variable weather influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of chance by averaging and the test of sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination of chance consists in repeating experiments and using the mean; the induction is sufficient when further repetitions do not materially alter the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practical rule for removing the influence of floating, unassignable causes (chance). It enables both quantifying the effect of a dominant cause and detecting small constant causes (residual phenomena). Examples: loaded dice detected by persistent deviation from expected mean; diurnal barometer variation discovered by comparing mean heights at different hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of residual phenomena by eliminating chance
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after sufficiently many trials, the average effect is non-zero (or deviates from the null expectation) and stable, conclude the presence of a constant cause producing the residual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the constant cause's effect is small relative to variable causes, a stable non-zero mean indicates its existence; follow with methods to detect the source. Example: detecting slight bias in dice or small diurnal atmospheric effects from averaging many observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and proper conception of chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance should be understood not as events without causes but as coincidences of phenomena for which we have no ground to infer a uniformity; two phenomena may be conjoined by chance (casually) if they are unrelated through causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is incorrect to say phenomena are produced by chance; rather their conjunction may be casual. Recurrence of a coincidence does not by itself prove it is lawful. Distinguish casual conjunctions (effects of unrelated causes) from causal connections, and remember that full enumeration of circumstances is required to claim repeatability implies law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability requires reduction to equally possible cases (Laplace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace: probability consists in reducing events of the same kind to a number of cases equally possible (equally undecided) and taking the ratio of favorable cases to all possible cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two preconditions are needed: (1) among the set, one and only one event will happen; (2) we have no reason to prefer one over another (equally undecided). Critics note an empirical-frequency foundation may also be required: equal undecision should be justified by observed equal frequencies in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for theory of chances to assess sampling deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond long-run expected frequencies, we must ask how large deviations from that average may credibly occur in smaller samples; this is the domain of the doctrine of chances (theory of probabilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To decide whether an observed deviation in a finite sample is compatible with chance, one must use the mathematics of probability to estimate the expected variation and the extremal limits; this supplements the marginal-frequency calculations used to detect causal connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of empirical laws varies with presumed resolvability
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws differ in authority according to whether there is reason to presume they are resolvable solely into laws or into laws plus collocations; those likely resolvable into simpler laws are of greater authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences in biological development (nutrition, organ functions) are empirical but likely resolvable into corpuscular laws and thus are relatively authoritative; uniformities like order of strata are weaker because they may depend on particular collocations without common causal origin.
